A typical request to the open model Kimi K3 emits about 0.4 grams of CO₂ in Sweden, 1.6 grams in Ireland, 2.5 grams in Germany and 3.2 grams in Texas, on identical hardware — 8.5 times more in Texas than in Sweden. page.text_excerpt: Matthias Endler Move Slow and Fix Things Last updated on 17th of August, 2024 Growing up as a kid in rural Bavaria, I always dreamed of moving to the US to run a startup. Many kids in my generation shared that dream. To me, it felt like the only way to combine my two greatest passions: writing code and building things. As I got older, I became disillusioned with the narrative surrounding Silicon Valley. The hockey stick growth, the VC money, the “get rich quick” mentality – it was all one big illusion. For a long time, I couldn’t put my finger on what exactly bothered me about it. Part of what made me increasingly uncomfortable was the glorification of hustle culture – the idea that you have to work yourself to the bone to make it big against all odds. The other part was the “winner takes all” mentality and the mindset that you have to “move fast and break things” to succeed. I don’t believe that has to be the case. As it turns out, I’ve always been drawn to the exact opposite: sustainable growth, robust solutions, and a long-term mindset. That’s why I’ve been contributing to open source for 15 years, why I only run small, bootstrapped businesses or non-profits, and why I focus on writing and knowledge sharing. Paul Graham and his VC buddies would have you believe that your ultimate goal as a founder should be to build a unicorn. page.text_excerpt: EWD 667 On the foolishness of "natural language programming". Since the early days of automatic computing we have had people that have felt it as a shortcoming that programming required the care and accuracy that is characteristic for the use of any formal symbolism. They blamed the mechanical slave for its strict obedience with which it carried out its given instructions, even if a moment's thought would have revealed that those instructions contained an obvious mistake. "But a moment is a long time, and thought is a painful process." (A.E.Housman). They eagerly hoped and waited for more sensible machinery that would refuse to embark on such nonsensical activities as a trivial clerical error evoked at the time. Machine code, with its absence of almost any form of redundancy, was soon identified as a needlessly risky interface between man and machine. Partly in response to this recognition so-called "high-level programming languages" were developed, and, as time went by, we learned to a certain extent how to enhance the protection against silly mistakes. It was a significant improvement that now many a silly mistake did result in an error message instead of in an erroneous answer. (And even this improvement wasn't universally appreciated: some people found error messages they couldn't ignore more annoying than wrong results, and, when judging the relative merits of programming languages, some still seem to equate "the ease of programming" with the ease of making undetected mistakes.) The (abstract) machine corresponding to a programming language remained, however, a faithful slave, i.e. the nonsensible automaton perfectly capable of carrying out nonsensical instructions. Programming remained the use of a formal symbolism and, as such, continued to require the care and accuracy required before. page.text_excerpt: Code and Cake Follow About me Docker is weird Oct 22, 2026 I decided to make my own container runtime for fun, and even though I’m still early on, I’ve learned that Docker is weird. Here’s some weird things I learned about Docker. Containers aren’t real Unlike VMs, containers are just processes with special restrictions on them. Your kernel is still running that process! And if you know where to look, you can even find that process in /proc. Containers really aren’t real There’s not really a linux feature that’s just “containers” either. Instead, containers are really 5 different linux kernel features in trenchcoat. Namespaces hide what the host and container can see, cgroups limit container resource usage, and there’s a whole bunch of networking magic I don’t understand that lets you isolate a container’s network. Images are just folders Images are just folders that Docker puts somewhere and then calls chroot (or pivot_root) to make that folder your container process’s new root directory. So if you run docker run -it --rm ubuntu /bin/bash, Docker is going to: Download the ubuntu image from Dockerhub. Put that image somewhere. Run /some/weird/docker/path/bin/bash Go is kind of a terrible language for a container runtime Docker’s container runtime, runc, is written in Go, and Go has some design choices that make it less suited for a container runtime. Go’s runtime is natively multi-threaded. That’s a really cool feature, but it leads to some challenges in runc. Many of the Linux syscalls a container runtime needs to make have to be done in a single-threaded environment, so runc has a crazy C module that runs before Go’s runtime initializes so it can run those syscalls. page.title: AI and The Enclosure of the Scientific Commons
page.description: The scientific literature can be viewed as an "information commons:" an intangible resource that "no one owns and is shared by everyone." There are well-established economic and political frameworks for understanding such commons, emerging from the history of agricultural common lands found in places like preindustrial England. This article provides a primer on the history and these frameworks, and considers a key difference between the information commons and the fields of yore: while information commons are robust and immensely valuable --- some can be said to rank among humanity's greatest achievements --- the English agricultural commons no longer meaningfully exist. The latter are gone not because of the well-known "tragedy of the commons," but rather a phenomenon known as the enclosure movement (~1600--1800) that transformed the common lands into private property. Many observers, then and now, judge enclosure to have been theft at a societal scale. This article argues that artificial intelligence (AI) provides precisely the tools needed to enable a previously-infeasible enclosure of the information commons. Although AI-enabled enclosure does not operate identically to physical enclosure, it shares the key features of turning the commons into private wealth and undermining the social systems that support them (via "slop spam"). The concepts presented in this article can provide a scholarly basis for interrogating the foreboding feeling that AI may represent not just a smash-and-grab, but an attack upon a whole way of life.

ZDI-CAN-33774 as a KSMBD race condition that can lead to remote code execution. Another CVSS 9.0 rated vulnerability. ZDI-CAN-33367 is a vulneravbility for skbuff skb_zerocopy in the network code that can lead to local privilege escalation. page.description: An interactive museum of ZFS, room by room: each idea of the OpenZFS source made visible, with the real code.
page.text_excerpt: Skip to content Uberblok Hall Rooms History Why this? Uberblok on GitHub EN English FR Français ES Español A museum of ZFS, read in its source Uberblok Storage has always had the same enemies: disks that lie, writes cut short, a crash in the middle of an update. ZFS answers them with a handful of ideas. This museum shows them one room at a time, from the code that implements them. Every animation maps to lines of OpenZFS zfs-2.4.4, frozen at commit 71a9f9578616, and every excerpt links to them. Nothing here is drawn from memory. Why this museum? ↓ 1 2 3 4 Fig. 1. The Hall’s object under the glass: struct uberblock, lines 122–128 of include/sys/uberblock_impl.h at zfs-2.4.4, printed with lines 36–150 of its file. struct uberblock: the record that names the whole pool ub_txg: the transaction group of the last sync ub_rootbp: the block pointer to the root of the tree, the MOS The listing: lines 36 to 150 of the file, numbered as in the source The object in the Hall: the uberblock A pool is millions of blocks spread over several disks. After a crash, the system must find its current, consistent state without scanning any of them. So one small record names the root of everything: the uberblock. It holds a transaction group number, ub_txg, and one block pointer, ub_rootbp; every other block of the pool is reachable from that pointer. Each disk carries four labels, two at its start and two at its end, and each label keeps a 128 KiB ring of uberblocks. A new uberblock never overwrites the previous one: the uberblock of txg N goes to slot N mod the number of slots (with multihost=on, the last slot is kept for MMP and the ring turns on one slot fewer). On import, ZFS reads every slot of every label and keeps the valid uberblock with the highest txg. The ring is often said to hold 128 uberblocks. It holds 128 KiB: a slot takes one sector, rounded up to 1 KiB and capped at 8 KiB, so 128 slots on 512-byte sectors, 64 at ashift 11, 32 on the 4K-sector disks of today, 16 beyond. C

Once a week, Jim sits down with his phone, logs in to his mother’s Facebook account, and scrolls through her feed. His goal is simple: serve his mother’s algorithm a steady stream of inoffensive content he thinks will delight her and make sure anything inflammatory or scammy-looking is stamped NOT INTERESTED. At this point, it has become routine. He’ll tap the LIKE button under posts about Dick Van Dyke’s birthday, a few photo albums uploaded by distant family members, and the occasional cute cat video while blocking long-defunct Obama fundraising pages and clips of AI-generated men speaking directly to “the older woman holding this phone.” Jim is a 48-year-old graphic designer who lives in Portland, Oregon, with his wife and two cats. On one of our first video calls this past summer, his faintly stubbled face appears next to his now-80-year-old mother, Gloria, whose feed he has actively curated since April. Where he is unassuming and clean-cut, Gloria radiates a free-spirited energy; her cropped white hair is tucked under a blue headscarf covered in white mandalas, and she wears a tie-dye T-shirt. The two have an easy rapport. Occasionally, they break into side chats or finish each other’s sentences. “It’s just nice having somebody that knows me so well that they can even communicate for me if I need them to,” Gloria tells me. I bemoaned the approach of putting an icon in every menu item by default which shipped with macOS Tahoe — but now it’s gone in Golden Gate! John Gruber wrote about this reversion back in June, including the fact that Apple’s new Human Interface Guidelines specifically call out Tahoe’s approach to menus as an example of what not to do on macOS. As the old saying goes, it takes a big man corporation to admit when they’re wrong. As I mentioned in my original post, one of the arguments I had in my quiver against this practice was “Apple doesn’t do it”. But once Apple started putting icons in all their menus in Tahoe, I lost a persuasive point in my argument. But now, I think I have an argument that’s even stronger than before! It’s no longer: “Apple doesn’t put icons in their menus.” It’s: “Apple tried putting icons in all their menus, and even they went back on it!” They designed it, shipped it, lived with it for a year, then publicly changed their guidance on it. To me, that’s a lot more persuasive than simply saying, “Apple doesn’t do this.” Choosing not to do something you’ve never done is one thing. Choosing not to do something you’ve done is experience. page.text_excerpt: Alberto Denia iOS App Developer HOME PORTFOLIO WRITING SERVICES Agentic Coding Software Engineering Product Design Code is clay now Alberto Denia ∙ Sep 25, 2026 In the Middle Ages of coding (that is, before November 2025), we coder-stonemasons spent our days meticulously carving code-stone into finished pieces. Stone is unforgiving, and modifying it remained difficult even as better tools improved things over time. Small corrections were okay-ish (some chiseling here, some patching there), but larger ones meant demolition, scaffolding and a careful plan pinned to the wall. Agentic coding has turned that around: code has become malleable. Even though it’s still made of the same underlying substance as medieval code, the cost of making a change has collapsed. That makes it behave like a different material entirely. Code is clay now. Working with clay Once code is clay, you can start modeling it. Slap some big blobs of code-clay into the rough shape you want and see how it feels. Don’t like it? It’s easy to reshape a part or even squash the whole thing and start over. When the overall structure feels right, you refine the way a sculptor does: from the general mass, to the mid-sized features, to the details. Modeling can be applied fractally, at any layer of the thing you’re building. page.text_excerpt: sean goedecke January 24, 2026 │ tech companies, how to, large codebases How I estimate work as a staff software engineer There’s a kind of polite fiction at the heart of the software industry. It goes something like this: Estimating how long software projects will take is very hard, but not impossible. A skilled engineering team can, with time and effort, learn how long it will take for them to deliver work, which will in turn allow their organization to make good business plans. This is, of course, false. As every experienced software engineer knows, it is not possible to accurately estimate software projects. The tension between this polite fiction and its well-understood falseness causes a lot of strange activity in tech companies. For instance, many engineering teams estimate work in t-shirt sizes instead of time, because it just feels too obviously silly to the engineers in question to give direct time estimates. Naturally, these t-shirt sizes are immediately translated into hours and days when the estimates make their way up the management chain. Alternatively, software engineers who are genuinely trying to give good time estimates have ridiculous heuristics like “double your initial estimate and add 20%“. This is basically the same as giving up and saying “just estimate everything at a month”. Should tech companies just stop estimating? One of my guiding principles is that when a tech company is doing something silly, they’re probably doing it for a good reason. In other words, practices that appear to not make sense are often serving some more basic, illegible role in the organization. The wily frontman of Twisted Teens dances onstage like a marionette emulating the moves of a 1950s entertainer in a leather vest—a loud, motley style to match his band’s Americana-imbued garage rock. He looks like he was born on the muddy stoop of a beloved punk house. Instead, he’s spent the past decade in this picturesque cottage with salmon-colored shutters and white roof brackets carved to resemble lace. Here, nestled between oak trees and yucca plants in the Holy Cross neighborhood, Hollywell found a place to live and turned it into a creative wellspring. Back in 2016, following the death of his longtime friend and former Bay Area musician Paul Woods, Hollywell wandered down to New Orleans to commiserate with fellow punks at a different squat-turned-communal house in Holy Cross. After a lifetime of train-hopping across the country, playing old-time fiddle music with strangers, and working odd jobs, he knew it was almost time to put down roots. While exploring the neighborhood, his dog, Betty, took off and sprinted through the open door of an empty house, sniffing around yet completely at ease. In the dirt by his feet was a crumpled For Sale sign. Hollywell approached the landlord, a 70-something weed kingpin and car repairman who ran the entire block, to buy the house with his life savings.
